title: Ham Radio For Dummies
description: Respond to the call of ham radio Despite its old-school reputation, amateur radio is on the rise, and the airwaves are busier than ever. That’s no surprise: being a ham is a lot of fun, providing an independent way to keep in touch with friends, family, and new acquaintances around the world—and even beyond with its ability to connect with the International Space Station! Hams are also good in a crisis, keeping communications alive and crackling during extreme weather events and loss of communications until regular systems like cell phones and the internet are restored. Additionally, it’s enjoyable for good, old-fashioned tech geek reasons—fiddling with circuits and bouncing signals off the ionosphere just happens to give a lot of us a buzz! If one or more of these benefits is of interest to you, then good news: the new edition of Ham Radio For Dummies covers them all! In his signature friendly style, longtime ham Ward Silver (Call Sign NØAX)—contributing editor with the American Radio Relay League—patches you in on everything from getting the right equipment and building your station (it doesn’t have to be expensive) to the intricacies of Morse code and Ohm’s law. In addition, he coaches you on how to prepare for the FCC-mandated licensing exam and tunes you up for ultimate glory in the ham radio hall of fame as a Radiosport competitor! With this book, you’ll learn to: Set up and organize your station Communicate with people around the world Prep for and pass the FCC exam Tune into the latest tech, such as digital mode operating Whether you’re looking to join a public service club or want the latest tips on the cutting edge of ham technology, this is the perfect reference for newbies and experts alike—and will keep you happily hamming it up for years!  if(window.mix_cs

title: Understanding HAM Radio: The Basics of Amateur Communication (The Practical Ham Radio Oper
description: What if you could communicate across town, across the country, or even across continents without relying on the internet or a cellular network? Understanding HAM Radio opens the door to amateur radio, a hands-on hobby built around curiosity, connection, and the power of radio waves. Whether you are completely new to the subject or simply want to understand how ham radio works, this practical guide helps make the airwaves easier to navigate. Discover what sets amateur radio apart from broadcasting and commercial communications, how signals travel, and why terrain, weather, time of day, and solar activity can all affect your contacts. Getting started can seem complicated, but it doesn’t have to be. Explore the purpose of licensing, the basics of license classes and exams, and the operating rules that help keep radio communication safe and orderly. Learn how to choose a first radio, antenna, and essential accessories without rushing into equipment you may not need. Then get ready to make your first contact. Follow the steps for preparing your station, listening before transmitting, finding a clear frequency, and carrying on a courteous on-air conversation. You’ll also get familiar with call signs, phonetic alphabets, signal reports, and the everyday practices that help operators communicate clearly. As your interests grow, explore the many ways to use amateur radio. Learn about voice, Morse code, and digital modes; local communication on VHF and UHF; and long-distance contacts on HF. Find out how repeaters, nets, and operating schedules help bring radio communities together, and see how computers, maps, propagation tools, and station logs can support your activities. title: Ham Radio for the New Ham: What to Do the Minute You Get Your Amateur Radio License
description: This is the amateur radio book you want on the very day you get your new ham radio license. (Of course, you can use it after that, too.) You’ve studied. You’ve passed the test. You’ve received your call sign. But what do you do next? This book will provide the answer. It contains the things they don’t tell you when you’re studying for your license, but that you need to know as soon as you’ve got it. It includes 34 easy projects to help you grow your identity as a Ham, buy and set up your first radio, overcome the obstacles to getting on the air, and become part of the amateur radio community around you. With this book you’ll avoid some of the mistakes beginners often make. You’ll never have to flail around, wondering what to do or how to do it. When you complete these projects you’ll not only have your amateur radio “ticket,” you’ll know how to use it. Written by Amateur Extra class ham radio operator, Stan W. Merrill, call sign AI7E, it picks out the key things you’ll use daily from among the many you had to study to get your license. title: Building Your Ultimate HAM Radio Station: A Step-by-Step Guide to Mastering Home Radio Set
description: Turn a corner of your home into a capable, comfortable ham radio station—and know what to do at every step along the way. Building Your Ultimate HAM Radio Station is a practical guide to planning, assembling, testing, and improving a station that fits your interests, space, and budget. Whether you’re preparing for your first setup or refining equipment you already own, you’ll find a clear path from initial ideas to confident on-air operation. Start by defining what you want to do explore particular bands, try voice or Morse code, experiment with digital modes, or prepare to support communications in your community. Then consider the realities of your location, available space, electrical service, antenna possibilities, licensing requirements, and budget. A thoughtful plan helps you choose equipment with purpose instead of making costly guesses. Explore the key parts of a station, including transceivers, power supplies, feed lines, connectors, microphones, keys, headsets, speakers, and computer interfaces. Learn how to compare options and build a staged equipment list that can grow with your experience. You’ll also discover how antenna choices, placement, feed lines, impedance, SWR, and practical site limitations affect station performance. From arranging an efficient operating position to routing cables and securing antennas, this guide emphasizes careful preparation and safe installation. Follow a logical process for connecting components, configuring your radio, checking antenna performance, and testing receive and transmit audio before taking to the air. Once your station is ready, build good operating habits. description: When the phones go down, can your family still reach each other? Cell networks jam, towers lose power and phones run out of battery. A pair of inexpensive radios and a written plan can keep a family connected, but only if you know which radios to buy, what needs a license and what to say when it matters. This beginner's guide explains it in plain language, with 28 clear black-and-white diagrams, checklists and printable forms. No experience required. Inside you will find: FRS, GMRS or ham radio – a side-by-side comparison of what needs a license, what it costs, how much power each service allows and which one fits your family Realistic range – line of sight, antennas, repeaters and how to test your own radios along your own routes Choosing radios – handhelds, mobile and base radios, weather radios and scanners, with a buying ladder from first purchase to full station A family communication plan – out-of-area contact, three meeting places, channels, a listening schedule and a wallet card, with a fill-in plan you can print Emergency power – batteries, power banks, solar and generator safety, with a worked example for counting how long your power will last Go-kits at three levels – grab bag, car kit and home station, with checklists How to talk on the radio – a four-part message format, a short script and how to call for help Weather radio and alerts – NOAA Weather Radio, SAME codes and other information sources Emergency nets – what ARES, RACES, CERT and SKYWARN are and how to get involved Practice drills – a 12-month drill calendar and scenario drills for outages, evacuation and separated families Next steps – how to apply for a GMRS license and where to explore amateur radio Written for families, preppers and anyone who has never used a radio. This is not a license exam
